name: Alfatradiol (Ell-Cranell Alpha)

lead: Alfatradiol is a topical form of 17-alpha-estradiol, applied to the scalp to slow pattern hair loss in men and women. It is sold in Germany and parts of Latin America, and users see it as a non-finasteride option.

It is described as blocking 5-alpha-reductase locally, lowering DHT in the scalp, and has weak estrogen-receptor activity. Reports describe it as slowing or stabilising loss rather than adding density. In a randomized comparison in 103 women, 2% minoxidil outperformed it.

paras: It is used as a liquid applied to the scalp, regularly and over the long term. People tend to use it alone or as a gentler alternative to minoxidil or oral DHT blockers.
Reported effects are mostly local itching or burning, attributed to the alcohol vehicle. Safety in pregnancy, breastfeeding and under 18 is unknown. It is not FDA approved.

angle.text: Alfatradiol is a scalp-applied weak estrogen that reduces local DHT activity, so follicles thin more slowly and more density is kept. Users apply it as a non-finasteride option for pattern hair loss in men and women. Trials describe slowed loss with little regrowth.

lead: Alfatradiol, also called 17-alpha-estradiol, is a stereoisomer of the main human estrogen, 17-beta-estradiol. It is applied to the scalp as a low-concentration ethanolic solution to treat androgenetic alopecia in men and women, and is sold in Germany and several Latin American countries under names including Ell-Cranell Alpha, Pantostin, Avixis and Avicis [1][2].
It has far weaker estrogenic activity than estradiol and is described as inhibiting 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme that makes DHT [1]. It is not FDA approved [2].
A randomized comparison in 103 women found minoxidil outperformed alfatradiol, and Wikipedia reports that alfatradiol slowed or stabilized hair loss without increasing hair density [1][3].
infobox: Germany and parts of Latin America
Prescription-only in the US; not FDA approved for hair loss

paras: Alfatradiol is used for mild to moderate pattern hair loss in men and women, applied to the scalp [1][2]. Wikipedia notes that, like other hair-loss treatments, it must be used continuously, and advanced alopecia responds poorly [1]. A related product, Ell-Cranell Dexa, combines alfatradiol with dexamethasone [1].

In the 12-month comparison of 2% minoxidil twice daily with 0.025% alfatradiol once daily (switched to minoxidil after 6 months) in women with androgenetic alopecia, minoxidil performed better [3]. Wikipedia summarizes that alfatradiol slowed or stabilized loss but did not increase density or thickness, while an earlier randomized double-blind study found it reduced hair loss without regrowth [1]. Grokipedia describes an open-label phase IV study in Korean women reporting increased density and diameter after 8 months [2]; this is from an AI-generated source and a study not independently cited here.

Wikipedia reports no systemic side effects in earlier work, with local burning or itching attributed to the ethanol vehicle and possible stimulation of sebum production. Safety in pregnancy, breastfeeding and under 18 is unknown, and leaflets advise against use in those groups [1]. Grokipedia reports local reactions in under 4% of users [2].

Alfatradiol binds estrogen receptors alpha and beta with lower affinity than estradiol and has roughly 100-fold lower estrogenic activity, so it has little feminizing effect [1]. It is described as inhibiting 5-alpha-reductase, reducing DHT formation in the scalp [1][2].

The key randomized study compared 0.025% alfatradiol with 2% minoxidil in 103 women over 12 months and found minoxidil superior [3]. Other human data are described only in secondary encyclopedia sources [1][2].

A 2017 study in aging male mice found systemic alfatradiol improved metabolic function without feminization, which Wikipedia describes as preclinical [1]. Neuroprotective effects have been studied in models [1][2].

timeline.event: Hair-loss studies of alfatradiol date to at least this year [1].
Randomized comparison with minoxidil in women with androgenetic alopecia published [3].
